title: PETIT CHAPERON ROUGE
work: Histoires ou contes du temps passé
source: Charles Perrault, « PETIT CHAPERON ROUGE », dans Histoires ou contes du temps passé. Avec des Moralitez (Paris, Claude Barbin, 1697) ; texte de l’édition originale d’après la transcription de Wikisource, orthographe de 1697 conservée. Prononciation : français standard moderne ; les graphies de 1697 sont lues selon l’usage moderne.
about: Perrault’s tale is the earliest printed telling of Little Red Riding Hood, and it ends where the Wolf finishes eating: there is no woodcutter, no rescue, and no one comes out of the Wolf alive. The verse Moralité that closes it says plainly what the story is for — a warning about the quiet, obliging, honey-tongued men who follow young women home — and it is part of the tale, not a comment added to it. The 1697 spelling stands as the book prints it: «estoit» for «était», «luy» for «lui», «sçavoir» for «savoir», and «&» for «et».

sentences.t: Il estoit une fois une petite fille de Vilage, la plus jolie qu’on eut sçû voir ;
sentences.say: Il était une fois une petite fille de Village, la plus jolie qu’on eut su voir ;
sentences.l: There was one time a little girl of a village, the prettiest that one could have seen;
sentences.i: Once upon a time there was a little village girl, the prettiest that could be seen;
sentences.n: «Il estoit une fois» is the storyteller’s fixed opening: «il» is the impersonal ‘it’, standing where English says ‘there’, «estoit» is the 1697 spelling of «était» ‘was’, and «une fois» is ‘one time, once’. Lectorium gives it the matching English formula, ‘once upon a time’, in every tale it opens (Cendrillon prints it «Il eſtoit», with the long s). «Vilage» is printed with one l and a capital, as common nouns often take one in 1697, and «de Vilage» has no article: it says what she is, a village child. «qu’on eut sçû voir» uses «sçavoir» (modern «savoir») with an infinitive in the sense ‘to be able to’: ‘that one could have seen’. «eut» is the imperfect subjunctive «eût», printed without its accent; French puts the subjunctive after a superlative like «la plus jolie», and the mood is part of the praise — the prettiest one could ever have hoped to see.

sentences.t: sa mere en estoit folle, & sa mere grand plus folle encore.
sentences.say: sa mère en était folle, et sa mère grand plus folle encore.
sentences.l: her mother was mad about her, and her grandmother madder still.
sentences.i: Her mother doted on her, and her grandmother even more.
sentences.n: «en» stands for ‘about her’, picking the girl up from the clause before, and «estre folle de» ‘to be mad about’ is said of fondness, not of madness. The witness prints «mere grand» here as two bare words, where a few lines later it prints «mere-grand» with a hyphen; both are the older word for ‘grandmother’, modern «grand-mère». «&» is the printer’s ordinary sign for «et» ‘and’, and it stands throughout the book.

sentences.t: Cette bonne femme luy fit faire un petit chaperon rouge, qui lui seïoit si bien, que par tout on l’appelloit le Petit chaperon rouge.
sentences.say: Cette bonne femme lui fit faire un petit chaperon rouge, qui lui seyait si bien, que par tout on l’appelait le Petit chaperon rouge.
sentences.l: This good woman had made for her a little red hood, which suited her so well that everywhere they called her the Little Red Hood.
sentences.i: The good woman had a little red hood made for her, which suited her so well that everyone called her Little Red Riding Hood.
sentences.n: «chaperon» is a hood — a small hooded cape drawn over the head and shoulders — and nothing in the French says anything of riding: ‘Riding’ is the English name’s own addition, kept here because it is the name the tale carries in English, while the literal line says plainly ‘the Little Red Hood’. «luy fit faire» is the causative «faire» with an infinitive, ‘made make for her’: she did not sew it herself but had it made. «fit» is a passé simple, the tense French keeps for narrative past, and it carries the whole tale; «seïoit» is the imperfect of «seoir» ‘to suit, to become’, a verb now little used. «par tout» is printed as two words for modern «partout» ‘everywhere’.

sentences.t: Un jour sa mere ayant cui & fait des galetes, luy dit, va voir comme se porte ta mere-grand, car on m’a dit qu’elle estoit malade, portes luy une galette & ce petit pot de beurre.
sentences.say: Un jour sa mère ayant cuit et fait des galettes, lui dit, va voir comme se porte ta mère-grand, car on m’a dit qu’elle était malade, portes lui une galette et ce petit pot de beurre.
sentences.l: One day her mother, having cooked and made some cakes, said to her, go see how your grandmother is carrying herself, for one has told me that she was ill, carry her a cake and this little pot of butter.
sentences.i: One day her mother, having baked some cakes, said to her: Go and see how your grandmother does, for I am told she is ill. Take her a cake and this little pot of butter.
sentences.n: «galetes» are flat country cakes, not biscuits; the witness prints the word with one t here and with two in the same sentence. «cui» stands for «cuit», the past participle of «cuire» ‘to bake, to cook’, printed without its final t; Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «comme se porte ta mere-grand» is ‘how your grandmother carries herself’, the ordinary French for asking after someone’s health. «va» and «portes» are «tu» imperatives, the form a mother uses to her child — the English is ‘you’ either way — and «portes» keeps an s that modern French drops.

sentences.t: Le petit chaperon rouge partit aussi-tost pour aller chez sa mere-grand, qui demeuroit dans un autre Village.
sentences.say: Le petit chaperon rouge partit aussitôt pour aller chez sa mère-grand, qui demeurait dans un autre Village.
sentences.l: The Little Red Hood set out at once to go to her grandmother’s, who lived in another village.
sentences.i: Little Red Riding Hood set out at once for her grandmother’s house, in another village.
sentences.n: «aussi-tost» is the 1697 spelling of «aussitôt» ‘at once’, with the s that a circumflex later replaced, the same exchange that lies behind «forest»/«forêt» and «arrester»/«arrêter». «chez sa mere-grand» is ‘to her grandmother’s’, «chez» naming a person’s house with no word for house. «demeuroit» is the imperfect of «demeurer» ‘to live, to dwell’, in the -oit spelling 1697 uses where modern French writes -ait.

sentences.t: En passant dans un bois elle rencontra compere le Loup, qui eut bien envie de la manger, mais il n’osa, à cause de quelques bucherons qui estoient dans la Forest.
sentences.say: En passant dans un bois elle rencontra compère le Loup, qui eut bien envie de la manger, mais il n’osa, à cause de quelques bûcherons qui étaient dans la Forêt.
sentences.l: In passing through a wood she met neighbour the Wolf, who had a great desire to eat her, but he did not dare, because of some woodcutters who were in the forest.
sentences.i: Passing through a wood she met Neighbour Wolf, who had a great mind to eat her, but did not dare, because of some woodcutters who were in the forest.
sentences.n: «compere» is properly the man who stands godfather to one’s child, and from there any familiar old acquaintance; the beast fables give the title to the Wolf and the Fox much as English fable gives them ‘Brother’ or ‘Neighbour’. Its exact tone here is not recoverable — the title is warm and a little sly at once — and ‘neighbour’ in both layers is as near as English comes. «avoir envie de» is ‘to have a mind to’. «n’osa» stands without «pas», which 1697 often leaves out after «oser»; «eut», «rencontra» and «osa» are passé simple. «Forest» and «bucherons» are the 1697 spellings of «forêt» and «bûcherons».

sentences.t: Il luy demanda où elle alloit ;
sentences.say: Il lui demanda où elle allait ;
sentences.l: He asked her where she was going;
sentences.n: «demander» is ‘to ask’ in the sense of putting a question, not of asking for something, and «luy» is ‘of her, to her’. «alloit» is the imperfect of «aller» ‘to go’, again in -oit.

sentences.t: la pauvre enfant qui ne sçavoit pas qu’il est dangereux de s’arrester à écouter un Loup, luy dit, je vais voir ma Mere-grand, & luy porter une galette avec un petit pot de beurre que ma Mere luy envoye.
sentences.say: la pauvre enfant qui ne savait pas qu’il est dangereux de s’arrêter à écouter un Loup, lui dit, je vais voir ma Mère-grand, et lui porter une galette avec un petit pot de beurre que ma Mère lui envoie.
sentences.l: the poor child who did not know that it is dangerous to stop to listen to a Wolf, said to him, I am going to see my Grandmother, and to carry her a cake with a little pot of butter that my Mother sends her.
sentences.i: the poor child, who did not know that it is dangerous to stop and listen to a Wolf, said to him: I am going to see my Grandmother, and to take her a cake with a little pot of butter that my Mother is sending her.
sentences.n: «la pauvre enfant» is feminine: «enfant» takes either gender, and the article alone says this child is a girl. «écouter» is ‘to listen’, kept apart from «entendre» ‘to hear’ throughout, and the verb returns twice more — in the Wolf’s answer about his ears and in the Moralité. «sçavoir» prints a ç that modern «savoir» does not have, and «arrester» an s where «arrêter» has a circumflex. The present «il est dangereux» steps out of the narrative past into a standing truth.

sentences.t: Demeure-t-elle bien loin, lui dit le Loup ?
sentences.l: Does she live very far off, said the Wolf to her?
sentences.i: Does she live far away? said the Wolf.
sentences.n: «Demeure-t-elle» turns verb and pronoun about to ask a question, with a -t- put in only to keep the two vowels apart. «bien loin» is ‘very far’, «bien» strengthening rather than meaning ‘well’. The witness sets the question mark at the very end, after the speech tag rather than after the question, and spells «lui» here where it prints «luy» nearly everywhere else.

sentences.t: Oh ouy, dit le petit chaperon rouge, c’est par de-là le Moulin que vous voyez tout là-bas, là-bas, à la premiere maison du Village.
sentences.say: Oh oui, dit le petit chaperon rouge, c’est par delà le Moulin que vous voyez tout là-bas, là-bas, à la première maison du Village.
sentences.l: Oh yes, said the Little Red Hood, it is beyond the Mill that you see away down there, down there, at the first house of the Village.
sentences.i: Oh yes, said Little Red Riding Hood, it is past the Mill you can see away over there, over there, at the first house in the Village.
sentences.n: «ouy» is the 1697 spelling of «oui» ‘yes’. «par de-là» is ‘beyond, on the far side of’ (modern «par-delà»). The doubled «là-bas, là-bas» is the child pointing off into the distance, and the English keeps the repetition. «premiere» is printed without the accent of «première».

sentences.t: Et bien, dit le Loup, je veux l’aller voir aussi ;
sentences.l: Well then, said the Wolf, I want to go and see her too;
sentences.i: Well then, said the Wolf, I will go and see her too;
sentences.n: «Et bien» (modern «Eh bien») is ‘well then’. «je veux l’aller voir» sets the object pronoun «l’» before «aller» rather than before «voir», the usual 1697 order where modern French says «je veux aller la voir»; the same forward shift comes back in this tale at «s’alla coucher» and «je la veux manger» elsewhere in the book. «vouloir» here is close to a plain intention, ‘I mean to’.

sentences.t: je m’y en vais par ce chemin icy, & toy par ce chemin-là, & nous verrons à qui plutost y sera.
sentences.say: je m’y en vais par ce chemin ici, et toi par ce chemin-là, et nous verrons à qui plutôt y sera.
sentences.l: I am taking myself off there by this road here, and you by that road there, and we shall see who will be there sooner.
sentences.i: I shall go by this road here, and you by that road there, and we shall see which of us gets there first.
sentences.n: «je m’y en vais» packs two small words into «s’en aller» ‘to go off’: «en» ‘from here’ and «y» ‘there’. «plutost» here is ‘sooner, first’ (modern «plus tôt»), not «plutôt» ‘rather’; the two were not yet kept apart in spelling. «toy» and «icy» are the 1697 spellings of «toi» and «ici». The Wolf says «toy», the «tu» form, to the child, while she says «vous» to him; both are ‘you’ in the English.

sentences.t: Le Loup se mit à courir de toute sa force par le chemin qui estoit le plus court,
sentences.say: Le Loup se mit à courir de toute sa force par le chemin qui était le plus court,
sentences.l: The Wolf set himself to running with all his strength by the road that was the shortest,
sentences.i: The Wolf set off running as hard as he could by the shorter road,
sentences.n: «se mettre à» with an infinitive is ‘to set about doing’, marking the start of an action. «de toute sa force» keeps the singular where English says ‘as hard as he could’. French has only «le plus court» where English can say ‘the shorter’ of two.

sentences.t: & la petite fille s’en alla par le chemin le plus long, s’amusant à cueïllir des noisettes, à courir aprés des papillons, & à faire des bouquets des petites fleurs qu’elle rencontroit.
sentences.say: et la petite fille s’en alla par le chemin le plus long, s’amusant à cueillir des noisettes, à courir après des papillons, et à faire des bouquets des petites fleurs qu’elle rencontrait.
sentences.l: and the little girl went off by the longest road, amusing herself with gathering hazelnuts, with running after butterflies, and with making posies of the little flowers that she met with.
sentences.i: and the little girl went off by the longer road, amusing herself gathering hazelnuts, running after butterflies, and making posies of the little flowers she came upon.
sentences.n: «s’amuser à» is ‘to pass the time with, to amuse oneself doing’, with no notion of a joke in it. «cueïllir» is printed with a diaeresis for modern «cueillir» ‘to gather’, and «aprés» with the accent the wrong way for «après». «rencontroit» is the same verb that met the Wolf a moment ago, used now of coming upon flowers.

sentences.t: Le Loup ne fut pas long-temps à arriver à la maison de la Mere-grand, il heurte :
sentences.say: Le Loup ne fut pas longtemps à arriver à la maison de la Mère-grand, il heurte :
sentences.l: The Wolf was not long in arriving at the Grandmother’s house, he knocks:
sentences.i: The Wolf was not long in reaching the Grandmother’s house; he knocks:
sentences.n: «estre long-temps à» with an infinitive is ‘to be long in doing’. «heurter» is ‘to strike, to knock’, and «heurte» is a present tense dropped into a narrative otherwise in the past, which quickens the scene; the English keeps it. «long-temps» is printed with a hyphen for modern «longtemps».

sentences.t: Toc, toc, qui est là ?
sentences.l: Knock, knock, who is there?
sentences.n: «Toc, toc» is the sound of the knocking, as English says ‘knock, knock’, and «qui est là ?» is the answer called from within. Both lines come again word for word when the girl arrives at the same door.

sentences.t: C’est votre fille le petit chaperon rouge, dit le Loup, en contrefaisant sa voix, qui vous apporte une galete, & un petit pot de beurre que ma Mere vous envoye.
sentences.say: C’est votre fille le petit chaperon rouge, dit le Loup, en contrefaisant sa voix, qui vous apporte une galette, et un petit pot de beurre que ma Mère vous envoie.
sentences.l: It is your girl the Little Red Hood, said the Wolf, counterfeiting his voice, who brings you a cake, and a little pot of butter that my Mother sends you.
sentences.i: It is your girl, Little Red Riding Hood, said the Wolf, disguising his voice, bringing you a cake and a little pot of butter that my Mother is sending you.
sentences.n: «fille» is both ‘daughter’ and plainly ‘girl’; the child is the old woman’s grandchild, so the word is loose here, and the English says ‘girl’. «contrefaire» is ‘to imitate, to counterfeit’, and «contrefaire sa voix» is the set phrase for disguising one’s own voice. «sa» does not say whose: it may be his voice, put on, or hers, copied, and the French holds both; the same words «sa voix» come back a few lines on, when he softens it, where the voice is plainly his own, which is why the English reads it so here too. The Wolf takes over the girl’s own words and so says «ma Mere» of a mother not his. «galete» has one t here where the girl’s own line prints «galette»; «envoye» is the 1697 spelling of «envoie».

sentences.t: La bonne Mere-grand qui estoit dans son lit à cause qu’elle se trouvoit un peu mal, luy cria, tire la chevillette, la bobinette chera, le Loup tira la chevillette, & la porte s’ouvrit.
sentences.say: La bonne Mère-grand qui était dans son lit à cause qu’elle se trouvait un peu mal, lui cria, tire la chevillette, la bobinette cherra, le Loup tira la chevillette, et la porte s’ouvrit.
sentences.l: The good Grandmother, who was in her bed because she found herself a little unwell, cried to him, pull the little-peg, the little-bobbin will fall, the Wolf pulled the little-peg, and the door opened.
sentences.i: The good Grandmother, who was in her bed because she was feeling a little unwell, called out to him: Pull the little peg, and the latch will fall. The Wolf pulled the little peg, and the door opened.
sentences.n: «chevillette» is a diminutive of «cheville» ‘peg, pin’, and «bobinette» a diminutive that seems to go with «bobine» ‘bobbin’; together they name a simple wooden door-fastening, but what each piece was and how it worked is not certain, and ‘latch’ in the English is a best guess. «chera» is the future of «choir» ‘to fall’, whose usual spelling is «cherra»; the witness prints one r both times, in the Grandmother’s call and in the Wolf’s. Whether the single r is the 1697 printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «tire» is the «tu» form, as one calls to a child at the door; the English stays ‘you’. «à cause que» with a clause is ‘because’, where modern French uses «parce que» and keeps «à cause de» for a noun; «se trouver mal» is ‘to feel unwell’, literally ‘to find oneself ill’. «luy cria» is ‘called to him or to her’ without saying which: the old woman believes she is answering her grandchild, and only the English has to choose.

sentences.t: Il se jetta sur la bonne femme, & la devora en moins de rien ;
sentences.say: Il se jeta sur la bonne femme, et la dévora en moins de rien ;
sentences.l: He threw himself upon the good woman, and devoured her in less than nothing;
sentences.i: He threw himself upon the good woman and devoured her in no time at all;
sentences.n: «en moins de rien» is ‘in less than nothing’, the French for ‘in no time at all’. «jetta» and «devora» are passé simple; «jetta» is the 1697 spelling of «jeta», from «jetter» for «jeter», and «devora» is printed without the accent of «dévora».

sentences.t: car il y avoit plus de trois jours qu’il n’avoit mangé.
sentences.say: car il y avait plus de trois jours qu’il n’avait mangé.
sentences.l: for there had been more than three days that he had not eaten.
sentences.i: for it was more than three days since he had eaten.
sentences.n: «il y avoit trois jours que…» is the French way of measuring time back from the moment of the story: ‘it was three days that…’, that is, ‘it had been three days since…’. «il y a» is literally ‘it there has’: the impersonal «il» ‘it’, the adverbial «y» ‘there’ and «avoir» ‘to have’. «n’avoit mangé» stands with «ne» and no «pas», as French regularly does in a clause hanging on «il y a … que». Whether that «ne» is a true negation shorn of its «pas» or the empty «ne» such clauses attract is disputed, and the sense is the same either way: three days had gone by with nothing eaten.

sentences.t: Ensuite il ferma la porte, & s’alla coucher dans le lit de la Mere-grand, en attendant le petit chaperon rouge, qui quelque temps aprés vint heurter à la porte.
sentences.say: Ensuite il ferma la porte, et s’alla coucher dans le lit de la Mère-grand, en attendant le petit chaperon rouge, qui quelque temps après vint heurter à la porte.
sentences.l: Then he shut the door, and went himself to lie down in the Grandmother’s bed, awaiting the Little Red Hood, who some time after came to knock at the door.
sentences.i: Then he shut the door and went to lie down in the Grandmother’s bed, waiting for Little Red Riding Hood, who some time after came and knocked at the door.
sentences.n: «s’alla coucher» sets the reflexive «s’» before «alla» rather than before «coucher», as «je veux l’aller voir» did a moment ago; modern French would say «alla se coucher». «se coucher» is ‘to lie down, to go to bed’. «en attendant» is the gerund of «attendre» ‘to wait for’, a verb that needs no preposition in French. «vint» is the passé simple of «venir».

sentences.t: Toc, toc, qui est là ?
sentences.l: Knock, knock, who is there?
sentences.n: The knock and the question return word for word, with the girl now standing where the Wolf stood.

sentences.t: Le petit chaperon rouge, qui entendit la grosse voix du Loup, eut peur d’abord, mais croyant que sa mere-grand estoit enrhumée, répondit, c’est vostre fille le petit chaperon rouge, qui vous apporte une galette & un petit pot de beurre que ma Mere vous envoye.
sentences.say: Le petit chaperon rouge, qui entendit la grosse voix du Loup, eut peur d’abord, mais croyant que sa mère-grand était enrhumée, répondit, c’est votre fille le petit chaperon rouge, qui vous apporte une galette et un petit pot de beurre que ma Mère vous envoie.
sentences.l: The Little Red Hood, who heard the Wolf’s big voice, had fear at first, but believing that her grandmother had caught cold, answered, it is your girl the Little Red Hood, who brings you a cake and a little pot of butter that my Mother sends you.
sentences.i: Little Red Riding Hood, hearing the Wolf’s deep voice, was afraid at first, but thinking her grandmother had a cold, answered: It is your girl, Little Red Riding Hood, bringing you a cake and a little pot of butter that my Mother is sending you.
sentences.n: «entendit» is ‘heard’, from «entendre», which the tale keeps apart from «écouter» ‘to listen’. «grosse voix» is a big voice, meaning deep and rough. «avoir peur» is ‘to be afraid’, literally ‘to have fear’. «enrhumée» is ‘having a cold’, from «rhume» ‘a cold’, and English has no single verb for it. The words are her own, which the Wolf had counterfeited a moment ago, and they come back almost unchanged; only the spelling shifts, «vostre» here where the Wolf’s line printed «votre».

sentences.t: Le Loup luy cria, en adoucissant un peu sa voix ;
sentences.say: Le Loup lui cria, en adoucissant un peu sa voix ;
sentences.l: The Wolf cried to her, softening his voice a little;
sentences.n: «adoucir» is ‘to soften, to sweeten’, built on «doux» ‘soft, sweet’ — the same root that gives the «loups doucereux», the honeyed wolves, of the Moralité. The witness sets a semicolon where a colon would introduce the words that follow.

sentences.t: tire la chevillette, la bobinette chera.
sentences.say: tire la chevillette, la bobinette cherra.
sentences.l: pull the little-peg, the little-bobbin will fall.
sentences.i: Pull the little peg, and the latch will fall.
sentences.n: The Wolf gives the Grandmother’s call back word for word, in her own words. «chevillette» is a diminutive of «cheville» ‘peg, pin’, and «bobinette» a diminutive that seems to go with «bobine» ‘bobbin’; together they name a simple wooden door-fastening, but what each piece was and how it worked is not certain, and ‘latch’ in the English is a best guess. «chera» is the future of «choir» ‘to fall’, whose usual spelling is «cherra»; the witness prints one r both times, in the Grandmother’s call and in the Wolf’s. Whether the single r is the 1697 printer’s or the transcription’s, Lectorium prints its witness unaltered. «tire» is the «tu» form, as one calls to a child at the door; the English stays ‘you’.

sentences.t: Le petit chaperon rouge tira la chevillette, & la porte s’ouvrit.
sentences.say: Le petit chaperon rouge tira la chevillette, et la porte s’ouvrit.
sentences.l: The Little Red Hood pulled the little-peg, and the door opened.
sentences.i: Little Red Riding Hood pulled the little peg, and the door opened.
sentences.n: The same line as before, with the girl in the Wolf’s place. «s’ouvrit» is the passé simple of «s’ouvrir», a reflexive where English simply says ‘opened’.

sentences.t: Le Loup la voyant entrer, luy dit en se cachant dans le lit sous la couverture :
sentences.say: Le Loup la voyant entrer, lui dit en se cachant dans le lit sous la couverture :
sentences.l: The Wolf, seeing her come in, said to her while hiding himself in the bed under the cover:
sentences.i: The Wolf, seeing her come in, said to her from where he lay hidden in the bed under the blanket:
sentences.n: «la voyant entrer» is ‘seeing her enter’, a participle doing the work of an English clause, and «se cachant» is the gerund of «se cacher» ‘to hide oneself’. «couverture» is the covering of the bed, the blanket or counterpane.

sentences.t: mets la galette & le petit pot de beurre sur la huche, & viens te coucher avec moy.
sentences.say: mets la galette et le petit pot de beurre sur la huche, et viens te coucher avec moi.
sentences.l: put the cake and the little pot of butter on the bread-bin, and come lie yourself down with me.
sentences.i: put the cake and the little pot of butter on the bread chest, and come and lie down with me.
sentences.n: «la huche» is the kneading-trough or bread-chest, the wooden bin that stood in a country kitchen for dough and for bread; no everyday English word is left for it. «mets» and «viens» are «tu» imperatives, the Wolf keeping the way an elder speaks to a child; the English is ‘you’. «moy» is the 1697 spelling of «moi».

sentences.t: Le petit chaperon rouge se deshabille, & va se mettre dans le lit, où elle fut bien estonnée de voir comment sa Mere-grand estoit faite en son deshabillé, elle luy dit ;
sentences.say: Le petit chaperon rouge se déshabille, et va se mettre dans le lit, où elle fut bien étonnée de voir comment sa Mère-grand était faite en son déshabillé, elle lui dit ;
sentences.l: The Little Red Hood undresses herself, and goes to put herself into the bed, where she was much astonished to see how her Grandmother was made in her undress; she said to her:
sentences.i: Little Red Riding Hood undresses, and goes and gets into the bed, where she was much astonished to see what her Grandmother looked like undressed. She said to her:
sentences.n: The telling slips into the present at «se deshabille» and «va», then back into the past at «fut», as it did at «il heurte». «en son deshabillé» turns the verb just used into a noun: «un deshabillé» is what one has on when undressed, so ‘in her undress’. «estonnée» is the 1697 spelling of «étonnée» ‘astonished’, and «bien» strengthens it. «comment … estoit faite» is ‘how she was made’, that is, what she looked like.

sentences.t: ma mere-grand que vous avez de grands bras ! c’est pour mieux t’embrasser, ma fille :
sentences.say: ma mère-grand que vous avez de grands bras ! c’est pour mieux t’embrasser, ma fille :
sentences.l: My grandmother, how you have big arms! It is the better to embrace you, my girl.
sentences.i: Grandmother, what big arms you have! The better to take you in my arms, my girl.
sentences.n: «que vous avez de grands bras !» is an exclamation in which «que» is ‘how’: ‘how you have big arms!’. «mere-grand» is the older word for ‘grandmother’ (modern «grand-mère»), and «embrasser», built on «bras» ‘arm’, is ‘to take in one’s arms’. The girl says «vous» to her grandmother and the Wolf answers with «t’», the «tu» an elder uses to a child; both are ‘you’ in the English. Four more turns follow, each on the same frame, changing only the part of the body and the verb.

sentences.t: ma mere-grand, que vous avez de grandes jambes ! c’est pour mieux courir mon enfant :
sentences.say: ma mère-grand, que vous avez de grandes jambes ! c’est pour mieux courir mon enfant :
sentences.l: My grandmother, how you have big legs! It is the better to run, my child.
sentences.i: Grandmother, what big legs you have! The better to run, my child.
sentences.n: «pour mieux» with an infinitive is ‘the better to’. The Wolf now says «mon enfant» ‘my child’ where he first said «ma fille» ‘my girl’, and the English follows the change.

sentences.t: ma mere-grand que vous avez de grandes oreilles ! c’est pour mieux écouter, mon enfant.
sentences.say: ma mère-grand que vous avez de grandes oreilles ! c’est pour mieux écouter, mon enfant.
sentences.l: My grandmother, how you have big ears! It is the better to listen, my child.
sentences.i: Grandmother, what big ears you have! The better to listen, my child.
sentences.n: «écouter» is ‘to listen’, not ‘to hear’ («entendre»), and the English keeps that. The verb runs through the tale: the girl did not know it was dangerous «s’arrester à écouter un Loup» ‘to stop and listen to a Wolf’, and the Moralité warns against «écouter toute sorte de gens» ‘to listen to all sorts of people’; ‘listen’ renders it in all three places. The frame of the exchange is as before.

sentences.t: Ma mere-grand que vous avez de grands yeux ! c’est pour mieux voir, mon enfant.
sentences.say: Ma mère-grand que vous avez de grands yeux ! c’est pour mieux voir, mon enfant.
sentences.l: My grandmother, how you have big eyes! It is the better to see, my child.
sentences.i: Grandmother, what big eyes you have! The better to see, my child.
sentences.n: «yeux» is the plural of «œil» ‘eye’. The frame of the exchange is as before.

sentences.t: Ma mere-grand, que vous avez de grandes dens ! c’est pour te manger.
sentences.say: Ma mère-grand, que vous avez de grandes dents ! c’est pour te manger.
sentences.l: My grandmother, how you have big teeth! It is to eat you.
sentences.i: Grandmother, what big teeth you have! To eat you.
sentences.n: «dens» is the 1697 spelling of «dents» ‘teeth’. The last answer drops both «mieux» and the pet name, and «te manger» is simply ‘to eat you’; the English drops them too.

sentences.t: Et, en disant ces mots, ce méchant loup se jetta sur le petit chaperon rouge, & la mangea.
sentences.say: Et, en disant ces mots, ce méchant loup se jeta sur le petit chaperon rouge, et la mangea.
sentences.l: And, in saying these words, this wicked wolf threw himself upon the Little Red Hood, and ate her.
sentences.i: And with these words the wicked wolf threw himself upon Little Red Riding Hood and ate her.
sentences.n: «en disant» is the gerund, ‘in saying, as he said’. «méchant» is ‘wicked’, a harder word in 1697 than the modern one, which has softened toward ‘naughty’. The tale stops here: nobody cuts the Wolf open, and the rescue familiar from later tellings is not in this book. «loup» is printed without the capital the witness has given the beast throughout.

sentences.t: MORALITÉ.
sentences.l: MORAL
sentences.n: Every tale in this book closes with a «Moralité», a moral in verse printed after the story, and several carry a second one besides. The verse is Perrault’s own and belongs to the tale; it is not an addition to it.

sentences.t:
ON voit icy que de jeunes enfans,
Sur tout de jeunes filles,
Belles, bien faites & gentilles,
Font tres-mal d’écouter toute sorte de gens,
Et que ce n’est pas chose estrange,
S’il en est tant que le loup mange.
sentences.say:
ON voit ici que de jeunes enfants,
Sur tout de jeunes filles,
Belles, bien faites et gentilles,
Font très-mal d’écouter toute sorte de gens,
Et que ce n’est pas chose étrange,
S’il en est tant que le loup mange.
sentences.l:
One sees here that young children,
Above all young girls,
Beautiful, well made and pleasing,
Do very wrong to listen to all sorts of people,
And that it is not a strange thing,
If there are so many of them that the wolf eats.
sentences.i:
One sees here that young children,
Above all young girls,
Beautiful, shapely and charming,
Do very ill to listen to all sorts of people,
And that it is no strange thing
If the wolf eats so many of them.
sentences.n: «ON» is set in capitals because it is the first word of the piece, as printers of the day opened a text. «que de jeunes enfans» is ‘that young children’, with «de» where English says nothing. «bien faites» is ‘well made’, said of a good figure, and «gentilles» in 1697 is ‘pleasing, well-bred’, nearer ‘charming’ than the modern ‘kind’. «S’il en est tant que le loup mange» is ‘if there are so many of them that the wolf eats’, on the impersonal «il en est» ‘there are of them’. «icy», «enfans», «tres-mal», «estrange» and «Sur tout» for «surtout» are all 1697 spellings. The French rhymes; the English does not try to.

sentences.t:
Ie dis le loup, car tous les loups ;
Ne sont pas de la mesme sorte ;
sentences.say:
Je dis le loup, car tous les loups ;
Ne sont pas de la même sorte ;
sentences.l:
I say the wolf, for all wolves;
Are not of the same kind;
sentences.i:
I say the wolf, for not all wolves
Are of the same kind;
sentences.n: «Ie» is «Je» ‘I’: 1697 printing keeps one capital for I and J and sets I for both, as it does again at «Iusque» below, while the small j is printed as usual («jeunes», «jusque»). «mesme» is the 1697 spelling of «même» ‘same’. French wraps the negative round the verb, «ne sont pas», so ‘all wolves are not of the same kind’ is ‘not all wolves are of the same kind’, which the idiomatic line says outright. The semicolon at the end of the first line falls between «tous les loups» and its own verb, where nothing should separate them; the pointing looks like the printer’s, and Lectorium prints its witness unaltered.

sentences.t:
Il en est d’une humeur accorte,
Sans bruit, sans fiel & sans courroux,
Qui privez, complaisans & doux
Suivent les jeunes Demoiselles
Iusque dans les maisons, jusque dans les ruelles ;
sentences.say:
Il en est d’une humeur accorte,
Sans bruit, sans fiel et sans courroux,
Qui privés, complaisants et doux,
Suivent les jeunes Demoiselles,
Jusque dans les maisons, jusque dans les ruelles ;
sentences.l:
There are some of them of a winning humour,
Without noise, without gall and without wrath,
Who, tame, obliging and sweet,
Follow the young Ladies
Even into the houses, even into the bedchambers;
sentences.i:
There are some of a winning temper,
Quiet, with no bitterness and no anger,
Who, tame and obliging and sweet,
Follow young Ladies
Right into their houses, right into their bedchambers;
sentences.n: «une ruelle» is not a lane here: it is the narrow space between a great bed and the wall, where a lady of fashion received her visitors while she was still in bed — so the line has these wolves following young women into the most private corner of the house. The word plainly means a narrow lane as well, and that reading is possible; Lectorium takes the bedside sense because the line moves inward, from the street to the house and then further in, and a lane would send it back out. «privez» is ‘tame’, said of an animal that has been gentled; «accorte» is ‘winning, affable’; «complaisans» is ‘eager to please’, without the smugness the English cognate has picked up. «fiel» is ‘gall’, the bitterness of the bile, and «courroux» is ‘wrath’. «Il en est» is again ‘there are some of them’. The witness prints «Iusque» with the I that stands for J and then «jusque» with a j in the same line. «Demoiselles» is the title of a young woman of rank.

sentences.t:
Mais, hélas ! qui ne sçait que ces loups doucereux,
De tous les loups sont les plus dangereux.
sentences.say:
Mais, hélas ! qui ne sait que ces loups doucereux,
De tous les loups sont les plus dangereux.
sentences.l:
But, alas! who does not know that these honey-sweet wolves,
Of all the wolves are the most dangerous.
sentences.i:
But, alas! who does not know that these honeyed wolves
Are the most dangerous of all wolves.
sentences.n: «doucereux» is built on «doux» ‘sweet’ and means sweet past honesty — the sugared manner of the smooth talker, and the word carries its own warning. The question is rhetorical, and the witness closes it with a full stop rather than a question mark. «sçait» is the 1697 spelling of «sait», from «sçavoir» (modern «savoir»). Here the Moralité says outright what it has been warning of: not the beast of the wood but the soft-spoken man who follows a young woman home, and who is the more dangerous for being pleasant.
